title: Asma's belt
hookLine: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma tears her waistband in two to tie the food bags, and is called she of the two belts (Bukhari)

cards: A food bag, a water skin, and no string. That's the whole problem in today's story, and it happens in a house in Mecca on the night two men are about to vanish.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr are leaving for Yathrib in secret. Somebody has to pack the food. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr's daughter, Asma, tells us what happened in that kitchen.
The meal is ready. The bags are ready. And there's nothing in the house to tie them shut.

teach.b: Here's the scene as Asma tells it. She prepared the journey food for the Prophet and her father. They looked for something to bind the food bag and the water skin, and found nothing.
So she said to her father, in effect: by Allah, I can find nothing to tie it with except my waistband.
And Abu Bakr answered: then tear it in two. Tie the water skin with one half and the food with the other. She did.
And from that night on, she says, she was called dhat al-nitaqayn: she of the two belts. No miracle, no clever plan.

A young woman uses the cloth already wrapped around her, and the great journey of the hijrah leaves the house tied shut with half of a waistband. Notice where she's standing, too. The men will be hidden in a cave.

Asma is the one still in the city, in the house the searchers will come to. The sirah tells of her carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed, so her part wasn't finished in the kitchen.
And her name doesn't remember a speech or a battle.

teach.h: A NAME FOR A PRACTICAL CHOICE.
teach.b: It remembers a quick, practical choice made with what was in reach.

Aisha's telling of the night, also in Bukhari, puts it a little differently: Asma cuts a piece of her belt rather than tearing it in two. Both keep the same picture: the bag closed with her own cloth.
The road to Medina didn't begin with what anyone wished they had. It began with what was there.

how: Muslims retell Asma bint Abi Bakr's part in the hijrah from Sahih al-Bukhari and know her by the name it gave her: dhat al-nitaqayn, she of the two belts.

o: a belt she wore as a sign of her faith
the waistband she tore to tie the food bags
the rope used to lower food into the cave

s: Asma left Mecca with the Prophet and Abu Bakr
she stayed in the city; the two men hid in the cave.
in Bukhari, Asma herself tells the story of the belt
she describes preparing the food and finding nothing to tie it with.
every report in Bukhari says she tore the belt in two
in Aisha's account she cut a piece of it; in Asma's own, she tore it in two.

games.q: you're Asma. the food is ready, the travelers leave tonight, and there's nothing in the house to tie the bags. what do you do?
o: send someone out to find rope.
tear your waistband in two and tie them.
let them go with the bags open.
games.why: Abu Bakr told her to tear it in two, one half for the water skin, one for the food, and the name stuck: she of the two belts.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because you don't have the right tool, the right time, or enough of something.
Then look at what's actually around you, in your room, your pocket, your day, and ask quietly: what here could tie this bag shut, not perfectly, just well enough to start?
If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with what is already in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Asma's belt. Torn in two on the night of the hijrah to tie the food and the water, it gave Asma her name: she of the two belts. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'she of the two belts', the name Asma was known by.

carryVoice: Your line: two belts. A name that lasted, earned with a torn waistband. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2979 (Asma prepares the food; nothing to tie it; 'tear it in two'; called dhat al-nitaqayn)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 (Aisha's account of the hijrah; Asma cuts a piece of her belt)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Asma brings food to the cave)
